speaker: Cooper
text: And I’m Anderson Cooper from CNN. We want to welcome you to Washington University in St. Louis for the second presidential debate between Hillary Clinton and Donald Trump, sponsored by the Commission on Presidential Debates. Tonight’s debate is a town hall format, which gives voters a chance to directly ask the candidates questions. Martha and I will ask follow-up questions but the night really belongs to the people in this room, and to people across the country who have submitted questions online.

speaker: Raddatz
text: The people you see on this stage were chosen by the Gallup Organization. They are all from the St. Louis area and told Gallup they haven’t committed to a candidate. Each of them came here with questions they wanted to ask, and we saw those questions for the first time this morning. Anderson and I and our team from ABC and CNN are the only ones who have seen them. Both candidates will have two minutes to answer each audience and online question. We hope to get to as many questions as we can, so we’ve asked the audience here not to slow things down with any applause. Except for now.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Ladies and gentlemen the Republican nominee for president, Donald J. Trump, and the Democratic nominee for president, Hillary Clinton. [applause]

speaker: Cooper
text: Thank you very much for being here. We’re going to begin with a question from one of the members in our town hall. Each of you will have two minutes to respond to this question. Secretary Clinton, you won the coin toss, so you’ll go first. Our first question comes from Patrice Brock. Patrice?

speaker: Question
text: Thank you, and good evening. The last presidential debate could have been rated as MA, mature audiences, per TV parental guidelines. Knowing that educators assign viewing the presidential debates as students’ homework, do you feel you’re modeling appropriate and positive behavior for today’s youth?

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: Well, thank you. Are you a teacher? Yes, I think that that’s a very good question, because I’ve heard from lots of teachers and parents about some of their concerns about some of the things that are being said and done in this campaign.

speaker: Cooper
text: Secretary Clinton, thank you. Mr. Trump, you have two minutes.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Well, I actually agree with that. I agree with everything she said. I began this campaign because I was so tired of seeing such foolish things happen to our country. This is a great country. This is a great land. I’ve gotten to know the people of the country over the last year-and-a-half that I’ve been doing this as a politician. I cannot believe I’m saying that about myself, but I guess I have been a politician.

speaker: Cooper
text: Thank you, Mr. Trump. The question from Patrice was about are you both modeling positive and appropriate behavior for today’s youth? We received a lot of questions online, Mr. Trump, about the tape that was released on Friday, as you can imagine. You called what you said locker room banter. You described kissing women without consent, grabbing their genitals. That is sexual assault. You bragged that you have sexually assaulted women. Do you understand that?

speaker: Donald Trump
text: No, I didn’t say that at all. I don’t think you understood what was—this was locker room talk. I’m not proud of it. I apologize to my family. I apologize to the American people. Certainly, I’m not proud of it. But this is locker room talk.

speaker: Cooper
text: So, Mr. Trump…

speaker: Donald Trump
text: And we should get on to much more important things and much bigger things.

speaker: Cooper
text: Just for the record, though, are you saying that what you said on that bus 11 years ago that you did not actually kiss women without consent or grope women without consent?

speaker: Donald Trump
text: I have great respect for women. Nobody has more respect for women than I do.

speaker: Cooper
text: So, for the record, you’re saying you never did that?

speaker: Donald Trump
text: I’ve said things that, frankly, you hear these things I said. And I was embarrassed by it. But I have tremendous respect for women.

speaker: Cooper
text: Have you ever done those things?

speaker: Donald Trump
text: And women have respect for me. And I will tell you: No, I have not. And I will tell you that I’m going to make our country safe. We’re going to have borders in our country, which we don’t have now. People are pouring into our country, and they’re coming in from the Middle East and other places.

speaker: Cooper
text: Thank you, Mr. Trump.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Right now, other nations are taking our jobs and they’re taking our wealth.

speaker: Cooper
text: Thank you, Mr. Trump.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: And that’s what I want to talk about.

speaker: Cooper
text: Secretary Clinton, do you want to respond?

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: Well, like everyone else, I’ve spent a lot of time thinking over the last 48 hours about what we heard and saw. You know, with prior Republican nominees for president, I disagreed with them on politics, policies, principles, but I never questioned their fitness to serve.

speaker: Raddatz
text: And we want to get to some questions from online…

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Am I allowed to respond to that? I assume I am.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Yes, you can respond to that.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: It’s just words, folks. It’s just words. Those words, I’ve been hearing them for many years. I heard them when they were running for the Senate in New York, where Hillary was going to bring back jobs to upstate New York and she failed.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Mr. Trump, Mr. Trump—I want to get to audience questions and online questions.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: So, she’s allowed to do that, but I’m not allowed to respond?

speaker: Raddatz
text: You’re going to have—you’re going to get to respond right now.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Sounds fair.

speaker: Raddatz
text: This tape is generating intense interest. In just 48 hours, it’s become the single most talked about story of the entire 2016 election on Facebook, with millions and millions of people discussing it on the social network. As we said a moment ago, we do want to bring in questions from voters around country via social media, and our first stays on this topic. Jeff from Ohio asks on Facebook, “Trump says the campaign has changed him. When did that happen?” So, Mr. Trump, let me add to that. When you walked off that bus at age 59, were you a different man or did that behavior continue until just recently? And you have two minutes for this.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: It was locker room talk, as I told you. That was locker room talk. I’m not proud of it. I am a person who has great respect for people, for my family, for the people of this country. And certainly, I’m not proud of it. But that was something that happened.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Can we please hold the applause? Secretary Clinton, you have two minutes.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: Well, first, let me start by saying that so much of what he’s just said is not right, but he gets to run his campaign any way he chooses. He gets to decide what he wants to talk about. Instead of answering people’s questions, talking about our agenda, laying out the plans that we have that we think can make a better life and a better country, that’s his choice.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Well, you owe the president an apology, because as you know very well, your campaign, Sidney Blumenthal—he’s another real winner that you have—and he’s the one that got this started, along with your campaign manager, and they were on television just two weeks ago, she was, saying exactly that. So you really owe him an apology. You’re the one that sent the pictures around your campaign, sent the pictures around with President Obama in a certain garb. That was long before I was ever involved, so you actually owe an apology.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Secretary Clinton, I want to follow up on that.

speaker: Raddatz
text: I’m going to let you talk about e-mails.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: … because everything he just said is absolutely false, but I’m not surprised.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Oh, really?

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: In the first debate…[laughter]

speaker: Raddatz
text: And really, the audience needs to calm down here.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: … I told people that it would be impossible to be fact-checking Donald all the time. I’d never get to talk about anything I want to do and how we’re going to really make lives better for people.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Because you’d be in jail. [applause]

speaker: Raddatz
text: Secretary Clinton…

speaker: Cooper
text: We want to remind the audience to please not talk out loud. Please do not applaud. You’re just wasting time.

speaker: Raddatz
text: And, Secretary Clinton, I do want to follow up on e- mails. You’ve said your handing of your e-mails was a mistake. You disagreed with FBI Director James Comey, calling your handling of classified information, quote, “extremely careless.” The FBI said that there were 110 classified e-mails that were exchanged, eight of which were top secret, and that it was possible hostile actors did gain access to those e-mails. You don’t call that extremely careless?

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: Well, Martha, first, let me say—and I’ve said before, but I’ll repeat it, because I want everyone to hear it—that was a mistake, and I take responsibility for using a personal e-mail account. Obviously, if I were to do it over again, I would not. I’m not making any excuses. It was a mistake. And I am very sorry about that.

speaker: Raddatz
text: OK, we’re going to move on.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: And yet she didn’t know the word—the letter C on a document. Right? She didn’t even know what that word—what that letter meant.

speaker: Cooper
text: We have to move on.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: You did that. Wait a minute. One second.

speaker: Cooper
text: Secretary Clinton, you can respond, and then we’ve got to move on.

speaker: Raddatz
text: We want to give the audience a chance.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: If you did that in the private sector, you’d be put in jail, let alone after getting a subpoena from the United States Congress.

speaker: Cooper
text: Secretary Clinton, you can respond. Then we have to move on to an audience question.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: Look, it’s just not true. And so please, go to…

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Oh, you didn’t delete them?

speaker: Cooper
text: Allow her to respond, please.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: It was personal e-mails, not official.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Oh, 33,000? Yeah.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: Not—well, we turned over 35,000, so…

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Oh, yeah. What about the other 15,000?

speaker: Cooper
text: Please allow her to respond. She didn’t talk while you talked.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: Yes, that’s true, I didn’t.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Because you have nothing to say.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: I didn’t in the first debate, and I’m going to try not to in this debate, because I’d like to get to the questions that the people have brought here tonight to talk to us about.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: And get off this question.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: OK, Donald. I know you’re into big diversion tonight, anything to avoid talking about your campaign and the way it’s exploding and the way Republicans are leaving you. But let’s at least focus…

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Let’s see what happens…[crosstalk]

speaker: Cooper
text: Allow her to respond.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: … on some of the issues that people care about tonight. Let’s get to their questions.

speaker: Cooper
text: We have a question here from Ken Karpowicz. He has a question about health care. Ken?

speaker: Donald Trump
text: I’d like to know, Anderson, why aren’t you bringing up the e-mails? I’d like to know. Why aren’t you bringing…

speaker: Cooper
text: We brought up the e-mails.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: No, it hasn’t. It hasn’t. And it hasn’t been finished at all.

speaker: Cooper
text: Ken Karpowicz has a question.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: It’s nice to—one on three.

speaker: Question
text: Thank you. Affordable Care Act, known as Obamacare, it is not affordable. Premiums have gone up. Deductibles have gone up. Copays have gone up. Prescriptions have gone up. And the coverage has gone down. What will you do to bring the cost down and make coverage better?

speaker: Cooper
text: That first one goes to Secretary Clinton, because you started out the last one to the audience.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: If he wants to start, he can start. No, go ahead, Donald.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: No, I’m a gentleman, Hillary. Go ahead. [laughter]

speaker: Cooper
text: Secretary Clinton?

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: Well, I think Donald was about to say he’s going to solve it by repealing it and getting rid of the Affordable Care Act. And I’m going to fix it, because I agree with you. Premiums have gotten too high. Copays, deductibles, prescription drug costs, and I’ve laid out a series of actions that we can take to try to get those costs down.

speaker: Cooper
text: Secretary Clinton, your time is up.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: So I want us to get to 100 percent, but get costs down and keep quality up.

speaker: Cooper
text: Mr. Trump, you have two minutes.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: It is such a great question and it’s maybe the question I get almost more than anything else, outside of defense. Obamacare is a disaster. You know it. We all know it. It’s going up at numbers that nobody’s ever seen worldwide. Nobody’s ever seen numbers like this for health care.

speaker: Cooper
text: Mr. Trump, your time…

speaker: Donald Trump
text: It is a disastrous plan, and it has to be repealed and replaced.

speaker: Cooper
text: Secretary Clinton, let me follow up with you. Your husband called Obamacare, quote, “the craziest thing in the world,” saying that small-business owners are getting killed as premiums double, coverage is cut in half. Was he mistaken or was the mistake simply telling the truth?

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: No, I mean, he clarified what he meant. And it’s very clear. Look, we are in a situation in our country where if we were to start all over again, we might come up with a different system. But we have an employer-based system. That’s where the vast majority of people get their health care.

speaker: Cooper
text: Secretary Clinton…

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: … get to do pretty much whatever they want, including saying, look, I’m sorry, you’ve got diabetes, you had cancer, your child has asthma…

speaker: Cooper
text: Your time is up.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: … you may not be able to have insurance because you can’t afford it. So let’s fix what’s broken about it, but let’s not throw it away and give it all back to the insurance companies and the drug companies. That’s not going to work.

speaker: Cooper
text: Mr. Trump, let me follow up on this.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Well, I just want—just one thing. First of all, Hillary, everything’s broken about it. Everything. Number two, Bernie Sanders said that Hillary Clinton has very bad judgment. This is a perfect example of it, trying to save Obamacare, which is a disaster.

speaker: Cooper
text: You’ve said you want to end Obamacare…

speaker: Donald Trump
text: By the way…

speaker: Cooper
text: You’ve said you want to end Obamacare. You’ve also said you want to make coverage accessible for people with pre-existing conditions. How do you force insurance companies to do that if you’re no longer mandating that every American get insurance?

speaker: Donald Trump
text: We’re going to be able to. You’re going to have plans…

speaker: Cooper
text: What does that mean?

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Well, I’ll tell you what it means. You’re going to have plans that are so good, because we’re going to have so much competition in the insurance industry. Once we break out—once we break out the lines and allow the competition to come…

speaker: Cooper
text: Are you going—are you going to have a mandate that Americans have to have health insurance?

speaker: Donald Trump
text: President Obama—Anderson, excuse me. President Obama, by keeping those lines, the boundary lines around each state, it was almost gone until just very toward the end of the passage of Obamacare, which, by the way, was a fraud. You know that, because Jonathan Gruber, the architect of Obamacare, was said—he said it was a great lie, it was a big lie. President Obama said you keep your doctor, you keep your plan. The whole thing was a fraud, and it doesn’t work.

speaker: Cooper
text: Thank you, Mr. Trump.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: … so that we will be able to take care of people without the necessary funds to take care of themselves.

speaker: Cooper
text: Thank you, Mr. Trump.

speaker: Raddatz
text: We now go to Gorbah Hamed with a question for both candidates.

speaker: Question
text: Hi. There are 3.3 million Muslims in the United States, and I’m one of them. You’ve mentioned working with Muslim nations, but with Islamophobia on the rise, how will you help people like me deal with the consequences of being labeled as a threat to the country after the election is over?

speaker: Raddatz
text: Mr. Trump, you’re first.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Well, you’re right about Islamophobia, and that’s a shame. But one thing we have to do is we have to make sure that—because there is a problem. I mean, whether we like it or not, and we could be very politically correct, but whether we like it or not, there is a problem. And we have to be sure that Muslims come in and report when they see something going on. When they see hatred going on, they have to report it.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Secretary Clinton?

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: Well, thank you for asking your question. And I’ve heard this question from a lot of Muslim-Americans across our country, because, unfortunately, there’s been a lot of very divisive, dark things said about Muslims. And even someone like Captain Khan, the young man who sacrificed himself defending our country in the United States Army, has been subject to attack by Donald.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Thank you, Secretary Clinton.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: First of all, Captain Khan is an American hero, and if I were president at that time, he would be alive today, because unlike her, who voted for the war without knowing what she was doing, I would not have had our people in Iraq. Iraq was a disaster. So he would have been alive today.

speaker: Raddatz
text: And why did it morph into that? No, did you—no, answer the question. Do you still believe…

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Why don’t you interrupt her? You interrupt me all the time.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Why don’t you interrupt her?

speaker: Raddatz
text: Would you please explain whether or not the Muslim ban still stands?

speaker: Donald Trump
text: It’s called extreme vetting. We are going to areas like Syria where they’re coming in by the tens of thousands because of Barack Obama. And Hillary Clinton wants to allow a 550 percent increase over Obama. People are coming into our country like we have no idea who they are, where they are from, what their feelings about our country is, and she wants 550 percent more. This is going to be the great Trojan horse of all time.

speaker: Raddatz
text: And, Secretary Clinton, let me ask you about that, because you have asked for an increase from 10,000 to 65,000 Syrian refugees. We know you want tougher vetting. That’s not a perfect system. So why take the risk of having those refugees come into the country?

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: Well, first of all, I will not let anyone into our country that I think poses a risk to us. But there are a lot of refugees, women and children—think of that picture we all saw of that 4-year-old boy with the blood on his forehead because he’d been bombed by the Russian and Syrian air forces.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: That’s not been debunked.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: So, please…

speaker: Donald Trump
text: That has not been debunked.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: … go to HillaryClinton.com and you can see it.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: I was against—I was against the war in Iraq. Has not been debunked. And you voted for it. And you shouldn’t have. Well, I just want to say…

speaker: Raddatz
text: There’s been lots of fact-checking on that. I’d like to move on to an online question…

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Excuse me. She just went about 25 seconds over her time.

speaker: Raddatz
text: She did not.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Could I just respond to this, please?

speaker: Raddatz
text: Very quickly, please.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Hillary Clinton, in terms of having people come into our country, we have many criminal illegal aliens. When we want to send them back to their country, their country says we don’t want them. In some cases, they’re murderers, drug lords, drug problems. And they don’t want them.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Thank you, Mr. Trump. I want to move on. This next question comes from the public through the Bipartisan Open Debate Coalition’s online forum, where Americans submitted questions that generated millions of votes. This question involves WikiLeaks release of purported excerpts of Secretary Clinton’s paid speeches, which she has refused to release, and one line in particular, in which you, Secretary Clinton, purportedly say you need both a public and private position on certain issues. So, Tu, from Virginia asks, is it OK for politicians to be two-faced? Is it acceptable for a politician to have a private stance on issues? Secretary Clinton, your two minutes.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: Well, right. As I recall, that was something I said about Abraham Lincoln after having seen the wonderful Steven Spielberg movie called “Lincoln.” It was a master class watching President Lincoln get the Congress to approve the 13th Amendment. It was principled, and it was strategic.

speaker: Raddatz
text: We’re going to get to that later. Secretary Clinton, you’re out of time.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: … with the Russians and other foreign powers.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Mr. Trump?

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Well, I think I should respond, because—so ridiculous. Look, now she’s blaming—she got caught in a total lie. Her papers went out to all her friends at the banks, Goldman Sachs and everybody else, and she said things—WikiLeaks that just came out. And she lied. Now she’s blaming the lie on the late, great Abraham Lincoln. That’s one that I haven’t…[laughter]

speaker: Raddatz
text: Thank you, Mr. Trump.

speaker: Cooper
text: We want to turn, actually, to the topic of taxes. We have a question from Spencer Maass. Spencer?

speaker: Question
text: Good evening. My question is, what specific tax provisions will you change to ensure the wealthiest Americans pay their fair share in taxes?

speaker: Cooper
text: Mr. Trump, you have two minutes.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Well, one thing I’d do is get rid of carried interest. One of the greatest provisions for people like me, to be honest with you, I give up a lot when I run, because I knock out the tax code. And she could have done this years ago, by the way. She’s a United States—she was a United States senator.

speaker: Cooper
text: Secretary Clinton, you have two minutes. The question was, what specific tax provisions will you change to ensure the wealthiest Americans pay their fair share of taxes?

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: Well, everything you’ve heard just now from Donald is not true. I’m sorry I have to keep saying this, but he lives in an alternative reality. And it is sort of amusing to hear somebody who hasn’t paid federal income taxes in maybe 20 years talking about what he’s going to do.

speaker: Cooper
text: Thank you, Secretary.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: And we’re going to make sure that nobody, no corporation, and no individual can get away without paying his fair share to support our country.

speaker: Cooper
text: Thank you. I want to give you—Mr. Trump, I want to give you the chance to respond. I just wanted to tell our viewers what she’s referring to. In the last month, taxes were the number-one issue on Facebook for the first time in the campaign. The New York Times published three pages of your 1995 tax returns. They show you claimed a $916 million loss, which means you could have avoided paying personal federal income taxes for years. You’ve said you pay state taxes, employee taxes, real estate taxes, property taxes. You have not answered, though, a simple question. Did you use that $916 million loss to avoid paying personal federal income taxes for years?

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Of course I do. Of course I do. And so do all of her donors, or most of her donors. I know many of her donors. Her donors took massive tax write-offs.

speaker: Cooper
text: So have you paid personal federal income tax?

speaker: Donald Trump
text: A lot of my—excuse me, Anderson—a lot of my write- off was depreciation and other things that Hillary as a senator allowed. And she’ll always allow it, because the people that give her all this money, they want it. That’s why.

speaker: Cooper
text: So can you—can you say how many years you have avoided paying personal federal income taxes?

speaker: Donald Trump
text: No, but I pay tax, and I pay federal tax, too. But I have a write-off, a lot of it’s depreciation, which is a wonderful charge. I love depreciation. You know, she’s given it to us.

speaker: Cooper
text: In the past…

speaker: Donald Trump
text: And, again, Bernie Sanders, it’s really bad judgment. She has made bad judgment not only on taxes. She’s made bad judgments on Libya, on Syria, on Iraq. I mean, her and Obama, whether you like it or not, the way they got out of Iraq, the vacuum they’ve left, that’s why ISIS formed in the first place. They started from that little area, and now they’re in 32 different nations, Hillary. Congratulations. Great job.

speaker: Cooper
text: Secretary—I want you to be able to respond, Secretary Clinton.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: Well, here we go again. I’ve been in favor of getting rid of carried interest for years, starting when I was a senator from New York. But that’s not the point here.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Why didn’t you do it? Why didn’t you do it?

speaker: Cooper
text: Allow her to respond.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: Because I was a senator with a Republican president.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Oh, really?

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: I will be the president and we will get it done. That’s exactly right.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: You could have done it, if you were an effective—if you were an effective senator, you could have done it. If you were an effective senator, you could have done it. But you were not an effective senator.

speaker: Cooper
text: Please allow her to respond. She didn’t interrupt you.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: You know, under our Constitution, presidents have something called veto power. Look, he has now said repeatedly, “30 years this and 30 years that.” So let me talk about my 30 years in public service. I’m very glad to do so.

speaker: Cooper
text: Thank you, secretary.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: And I’ve proven that I can, and for 30 years, I’ve produced results for people.

speaker: Cooper
text: Thank you, secretary.

speaker: Raddatz
text: We’re going to move on to Syria. Both of you have mentioned that.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: She said a lot of things that were false. I mean, I think we should be allowed to maybe…

speaker: Raddatz
text: No, we can—no, Mr. Trump, we’re going to go on. This is about the audience.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Excuse me. Because she has been a disaster as a senator. A disaster.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Mr. Trump, we’re going to move on. The heart-breaking video of a 5-year-old Syrian boy named Omran sitting in an ambulance after being pulled from the rubble after an air strike in Aleppo focused the world’s attention on the horrors of the war in Syria, with 136 million views on Facebook alone.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: Well, the situation in Syria is catastrophic. And every day that goes by, we see the results of the regime by Assad in partnership with the Iranians on the ground, the Russians in the air, bombarding places, in particular Aleppo, where there are hundreds of thousands of people, probably about 250,000 still left. And there is a determined effort by the Russian air force to destroy Aleppo in order to eliminate the last of the Syrian rebels who are really holding out against the Assad regime.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Thank you, Secretary Clinton. Mr. Trump?

speaker: Donald Trump
text: First of all, she was there as secretary of state with the so-called line in the sand, which…

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: No, I wasn’t. I was gone. I hate to interrupt you, but at some point…

speaker: Donald Trump
text: OK. But you were in contact—excuse me. You were…

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: At some point, we need to do some fact-checking here.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: You were in total contact with the White House, and perhaps, sadly, Obama probably still listened to you. I don’t think he would be listening to you very much anymore.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Mr. Trump, Mr. Trump, your two minutes is up.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: And one thing I have to say.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Your two minutes is up.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: I don’t like Assad at all, but Assad is killing ISIS. Russia is killing ISIS. And Iran is killing ISIS. And those three have now lined up because of our weak foreign policy.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Mr. Trump, let me repeat the question. If you were president…[laughter]…what would you do about Syria and the humanitarian crisis in Aleppo? And I want to remind you what your running mate said. He said provocations by Russia need to be met with American strength and that if Russia continues to be involved in air strikes along with the Syrian government forces of Assad, the United States of America should be prepared to use military force to strike the military targets of the Assad regime.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: OK. He and I haven’t spoken, and I disagree. I disagree.

speaker: Raddatz
text: You disagree with your running mate?

speaker: Donald Trump
text: I think you have to knock out ISIS. Right now, Syria is fighting ISIS. We have people that want to fight both at the same time. But Syria is no longer Syria. Syria is Russia and it’s Iran, who she made strong and Kerry and Obama made into a very powerful nation and a very rich nation, very, very quickly, very, very quickly.

speaker: Raddatz
text: What do you think will happen if Aleppo falls?

speaker: Donald Trump
text: I think Aleppo is a disaster, humanitarian-wise.

speaker: Raddatz
text: What do you think will happen if it falls?

speaker: Donald Trump
text: I think that it basically has fallen. OK? It basically has fallen. Let me tell you something. You take a look at Mosul. The biggest problem I have with the stupidity of our foreign policy, we have Mosul. They think a lot of the ISIS leaders are in Mosul. So we have announcements coming out of Washington and coming out of Iraq, we will be attacking Mosul in three weeks or four weeks.

speaker: Raddatz
text: There are sometimes reasons the military does that. Psychological warfare.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: I can’t think of any. I can’t think of any. And I’m pretty good at it.

speaker: Raddatz
text: It might be to help get civilians out.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: And we have General Flynn. And we have—look, I have 200 generals and admirals who endorsed me. I have 21 Congressional Medal of Honor recipients who endorsed me. We talk about it all the time. They understand, why can’t they do something secretively, where they go in and they knock out the leadership? How—why would these people stay there? I’ve been reading now…

speaker: Raddatz
text: Tell me what your strategy is.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: … for weeks—I’ve been reading now for weeks about Mosul, that it’s the harbor of where—you know, between Raqqa and Mosul, this is where they think the ISIS leaders are. Why would they be saying—they’re not staying there anymore. They’re gone. Because everybody’s talking about how Iraq, which is us with our leadership, goes in to fight Mosul.

speaker: Raddatz
text: I’m going to go to Secretary Clinton. Secretary Clinton, you want Assad to go. You advocated arming rebels, but it looks like that may be too late for Aleppo. You talk about diplomatic efforts. Those have failed. Cease-fires have failed. Would you introduce the threat of U.S. military force beyond a no-fly zone against the Assad regime to back up diplomacy?

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: I would not use American ground forces in Syria. I think that would be a very serious mistake. I don’t think American troops should be holding territory, which is what they would have to do as an occupying force. I don’t think that is a smart strategy.

speaker: Raddatz
text: But what would you do differently than President Obama is doing?

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: Well, Martha, I hope that by the time I—if I’m fortunate…

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Everything.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: I hope by the time I am president that we will have pushed ISIS out of Iraq. I do think that there is a good chance that we can take Mosul. And, you know, Donald says he knows more about ISIS than the generals. No, he doesn’t.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Thank you very much. We’re going to move on…

speaker: Donald Trump
text: You know what’s funny? She went over a minute over, and you don’t stop her. When I go one second over, it’s like a big deal.

speaker: Raddatz
text: You had many answers.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: It’s really—it’s really very interesting.

speaker: Cooper
text: We’ve got a question over here from James Carter. Mr. Carter?

speaker: Question
text: My question is, do you believe you can be a devoted president to all the people in the United States?

speaker: Cooper
text: That question begins for Mr. Trump.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Absolutely. I mean, she calls our people deplorable, a large group, and irredeemable. I will be a president for all of our people. And I’ll be a president that will turn our inner cities around and will give strength to people and will give economics to people and will bring jobs back.

speaker: Cooper
text: Mr. Trump, thank you.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: But I will tell you, she’s all talk. It doesn’t get done. All you have to do is take a look at her Senate run. Take a look at upstate New York.

speaker: Cooper
text: Your two minutes is up. Secretary Clinton, two minutes?

speaker: Donald Trump
text: It turned out to be a disaster.

speaker: Cooper
text: You have two minutes, Secretary Clinton.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: Well, 67 percent of the people voted to re-elect me when I ran for my second term, and I was very proud and very humbled by that.

speaker: Cooper
text: Your time, Secretary Clinton.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: Democrats, Republicans, independents, people across our country. If you don’t vote for me, I still want to be your president.

speaker: Cooper
text: Your two minutes is up.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: I want to be the best president I can be for every American.

speaker: Cooper
text: Secretary Clinton, your two minutes is up. I want to follow up on something that Donald Trump actually said to you, a comment you made last month. You said that half of Donald Trump’s supporters are, quote, “deplorables, racist, sexist, homophobic, xenophobic, Islamophobic.” You later said you regretted saying half. You didn’t express regret for using the term “deplorables.” To Mr. Carter’s question, how can you unite a country if you’ve written off tens of millions of Americans?

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: Well, within hours I said that I was sorry about the way I talked about that, because my argument is not with his supporters. It’s with him and with the hateful and divisive campaign that he has run, and the inciting of violence at his rallies, and the very brutal kinds of comments about not just women, but all Americans, all kinds of Americans.

speaker: Cooper
text: Thank you.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: Because we talked about what we wanted to do. We might have had some differences, and we had a lot of debates…

speaker: Cooper
text: Thank you, Secretary.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: … but we believed that we could make the country better. And I was proud of that.

speaker: Cooper
text: I want to give you a minute to respond.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: We have a divided nation. We have a very divided nation. You look at Charlotte. You look at Baltimore. You look at the violence that’s taking place in the inner cities, Chicago, you take a look at Washington, D.C.

speaker: Cooper
text: She said some of them are irredeemable.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: She’s got tremendous—she’s got tremendous hatred. And this country cannot take another four years of Barack Obama, and that’s what you’re getting with her.

speaker: Cooper
text: Mr. Trump, let me follow up with you. In 2008, you wrote in one of your books that the most important characteristic of a good leader is discipline. You said, if a leader doesn’t have it, quote, “he or she won’t be one for very long.” In the days after the first debate, you sent out a series of tweets from 3 a.m. to 5 a.m., including one that told people to check out a sex tape. Is that the discipline of a good leader?

speaker: Donald Trump
text: No, there wasn’t check out a sex tape. It was just take a look at the person that she built up to be this wonderful Girl Scout who was no Girl Scout.

speaker: Cooper
text: You mentioned sex tape.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: By the way, just so you understand, when she said 3 o’clock in the morning, take a look at Benghazi. She said who is going to answer the call at 3 o’clock in the morning? Guess what? She didn’t answer it, because when Ambassador Stevens…

speaker: Cooper
text: The question is, is that the discipline of a good leader?

speaker: Donald Trump
text: … 600—wait a minute, Anderson, 600 times. Well, she said she was awake at 3 o’clock in the morning, and she also sent a tweet out at 3 o’clock in the morning, but I won’t even mention that. But she said she’ll be awake. Who’s going—the famous thing, we’re going to answer our call at 3 o’clock in the morning. Guess what happened? Ambassador Stevens—Ambassador Stevens sent 600 requests for help. And the only one she talked to was Sidney Blumenthal, who’s her friend and not a good guy, by the way. So, you know, she shouldn’t be talking about that.

speaker: Cooper
text: Secretary Clinton, does Mr. Trump have the discipline to be a good leader?

speaker: Donald Trump
text: I’m shocked to hear that. [laughter]

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: Well, it’s not only my opinion. It’s the opinion of many others, national security experts, Republicans, former Republican members of Congress. But it’s in part because those of us who have had the great privilege of seeing this job up close and know how difficult it is, and it’s not just because I watched my husband take a $300 billion deficit and turn it into a $200 billion surplus, and 23 million new jobs were created, and incomes went up for everybody. Everybody. African-American incomes went up 33 percent.

speaker: Cooper
text: We have to move along.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: Nine million people lost their jobs.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Secretary Clinton, we have to…

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: Five million homes were lost.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Secretary Clinton, we’re moving on.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: And $13 trillion in family wealth was wiped out. We are back on the right track. He would send us back into recession with his tax plans that benefit the wealthiest of Americans.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Secretary Clinton, we are moving to an audience question. We’re almost out of time. We have another…

speaker: Donald Trump
text: We have the slowest growth since 1929.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Mr. Trump, we’re moving to an audience question.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: It is—our country has the slowest growth and jobs are a disaster.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Mr. Trump, Secretary Clinton, we want to get to the audience. Thank you very much both of you. [laughter]

speaker: Question
text: Good evening. Perhaps the most important aspect of this election is the Supreme Court justice. What would you prioritize as the most important aspect of selecting a Supreme Court justice?

speaker: Raddatz
text: We begin with your two minutes, Secretary Clinton.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: Thank you. Well, you’re right. This is one of the most important issues in this election. I want to appoint Supreme Court justices who understand the way the world really works, who have real-life experience, who have not just been in a big law firm and maybe clerked for a judge and then gotten on the bench, but, you know, maybe they tried some more cases, they actually understand what people are up against.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Thank you, Secretary Clinton. Thank you. You’re out of time. Mr. Trump?

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Justice Scalia, great judge, died recently. And we have a vacancy. I am looking to appoint judges very much in the mold of Justice Scalia. I’m looking for judges—and I’ve actually picked 20 of them so that people would see, highly respected, highly thought of, and actually very beautifully reviewed by just about everybody.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: Well…[crosstalk]

speaker: Raddatz
text: Thank you very much. We’re going to get on to one more question.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: The question was about the Supreme Court. And I just want to quickly say, I respect the Second Amendment. But I believe there should be comprehensive background checks, and we should close the gun show loophole, and close the online loophole.

speaker: Cooper
text: Thank you.

speaker: Raddatz
text: We have—we have one more question, Mrs. Clinton.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: We have to save as many lives as we possibly can.

speaker: Cooper
text: We have one more question from Ken Bone about energy policy. Ken?

speaker: Question
text: What steps will your energy policy take to meet our energy needs, while at the same time remaining environmentally friendly and minimizing job loss for fossil power plant workers?

speaker: Cooper
text: Mr. Trump, two minutes?

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Absolutely. I think it’s such a great question, because energy is under siege by the Obama administration. Under absolutely siege. The EPA, Environmental Protection Agency, is killing these energy companies. And foreign companies are now coming in buying our—buying so many of our different plants and then re-jiggering the plant so that they can take care of their oil.

speaker: Cooper
text: Your time is up. Thank you.

speaker: Donald Trump
text: It’s an absolute disgrace.

speaker: Cooper
text: Secretary Clinton, two minutes.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: And actually—well, that was very interesting. First of all, China is illegally dumping steel in the United States and Donald Trump is buying it to build his buildings, putting steelworkers and American steel plants out of business. That’s something that I fought against as a senator and that I would have a trade prosecutor to make sure that we don’t get taken advantage of by China on steel or anything else.

speaker: Cooper
text: Secretary Clinton…

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: But the price of coal is down worldwide. So we have to look at this comprehensively.

speaker: Cooper
text: Your time is up.

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: And that’s exactly what I have proposed. I hope you will go to HillaryClinton.com and look at my entire policy.

speaker: Cooper
text: Time is up. We have time for one more…

speaker: Cooper
text: One more audience question.

speaker: Raddatz
text: We’ve sneaked in one more question, and it comes from Karl Becker.

speaker: Question
text: Good evening. My question to both of you is, regardless of the current rhetoric, would either of you name one positive thing that you respect in one another? [applause]

speaker: Raddatz
text: Mr. Trump, would you like to go first?

speaker: Bill Clinton
text: Well, I certainly will, because I think that’s a very fair and important question. Look, I respect his children. His children are incredibly able and devoted, and I think that says a lot about Donald. I don’t agree with nearly anything else he says or does, but I do respect that. And I think that is something that as a mother and a grandmother is very important to me.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Mr. Trump?

speaker: Donald Trump
text: Well, I consider her statement about my children to be a very nice compliment. I don’t know if it was meant to be a compliment, but it is a great—I’m very proud of my children. And they’ve done a wonderful job, and they’ve been wonderful, wonderful kids. So I consider that a compliment.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Thanks to both of you.

speaker: Cooper
text: We want to thank both the candidates. We want to thank the university here. This concludes the town hall meeting. Our thanks to the candidates, the commission, Washington University, and to everybody who watched.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Please tune in on October 19th for the final presidential debate that will take place at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas. Good night, everyone.
